```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines); pair with fig.height
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# fill-in table drawn with base graphics so row height is controllable;
# body = list of rows, each a list/vector of cell strings ("" = blank)
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    fnt <- if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val,
                                    font = if (is_ans) 3 else fnt, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. Emits nothing in non-LaTeX output. lines =
# lines of prompt text, rows = rows of blank space below it (0.3 in each),
# extra = any other height (in inches), e.g. a figure or table
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}

ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
ponds <- read.csv("../../data/BdRegionalSurvey.csv")
X <- scale(as.matrix(ponds[, 2:9]))
pos <- ponds$bd_positive
n_frogs <- ponds$frogs_swabbed

# ridge-penalized NLL; par = c(beta0, beta1..beta8); beta0 not penalized
ridge_nll <- function(par, lambda) {
  p <- plogis(par[1] + X %*% par[-1])
  -sum(dbinom(pos, n_frogs, p, log = TRUE)) + lambda * sum(par[-1]^2)
}
ridge_fit <- function(lambda) optim(rep(0, 9), ridge_nll, lambda = lambda, method = "BFGS")$par
b0 <- ridge_fit(0)
b10 <- ridge_fit(10)
f2 <- function(v) formatC(round(v, 2) + 0, format = "f", digits = 2)   # + 0 drops "-0.00"

# answers: ridge path, lasso at lambda.1se, and 5-fold CV for the ridge lambda
library(glmnet)
lambda_grid <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100)
path <- sapply(lambda_grid, ridge_fit)
set.seed(1)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, cbind(n_frogs - pos, pos), family = "binomial", nfolds = 10)
b_lasso <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")[, 1]
held_out_nll <- function(par, rows) {
  p <- plogis(par[1] + X[rows, , drop = FALSE] %*% par[-1])
  -sum(dbinom(pos[rows], n_frogs[rows], p, log = TRUE))
}
set.seed(1)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(X)))
cv_lambdas <- c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)
cv_score <- sapply(cv_lambdas, function(lam) {
  sum(sapply(1:5, function(k) {
    train <- folds != k
    par <- optim(rep(0, 9), function(b) {
      p <- plogis(b[1] + X[train, ] %*% b[-1])
      -sum(dbinom(pos[train], n_frogs[train], p, log = TRUE)) + lam * sum(b[-1]^2)
    }, method = "BFGS")$par
    held_out_nll(par, !train)
  }))
})
best_lambda <- cv_lambdas[which.min(cv_score)]
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

## The scenario

In Act 1 you compared seven hand-picked models for Bd prevalence in the
60-pond survey. With eight candidate pond features there are $2^8 = 256$
possible subsets, and AIC couldn't separate temperature from elevation.
Another approach is to keep all eight features in one model and
**penalize** the size of their coefficients, so a feature keeps a
large coefficient only if the data insist on it.

**What happens to each pond feature's coefficient when all eight
compete, and what can we tell the managers?**

Try Part 1 on paper first, before you open a laptop or start typing
code.

`r nq(6, 6)`

## Part 1: Plan it on paper (~15 min)

**1a.** Write the ridge-penalized NLL for the logistic-binomial model
with all eight standardized predictors, as a function of
$\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_8$ and the penalty $\lambda$. Should
$\beta_0$ be penalized? Why or why not?

\ansbegin

$$\text{PNLL}(\beta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{60} \left[ y_i \log p_i + (n_i - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \right]
  + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{8} \beta_j^2 + \text{const.}, \qquad
  \text{logit}(p_i) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{8} \beta_j x_{ij}$$

No: $\beta_0$ sets the overall prevalence. Shrinking it toward 0 would
pull every pond's prevalence toward 50% for no reason.

\ansend

`r nq(3, 3)`

**1b.** Why standardize the predictors before penalizing them?

\ansbegin

One penalty applies to every coefficient, but a raw coefficient's size
depends on units (per meter of elevation vs. per °C). Standardizing
puts every coefficient on the same per-SD scale, so the penalty treats
them alike.

\ansend

`r nq(5, 8)`

**1c.** In plain English (not R code), describe step by step how you
would choose $\lambda$ for your ridge model by 5-fold cross-validation,
scoring each held-out fold by its NLL.

\ansbegin

Randomly split the 60 ponds into 5 groups of 12. For each candidate
$\lambda$ in a grid: for each group in turn, fit the ridge model to
the other 48 ponds, then compute the (unpenalized) NLL of the 12
held-out ponds using those coefficients; add up the 5 held-out NLLs.
Choose the $\lambda$ with the smallest total.

\ansend

`r nq(3, 0)`

`r nq(8, 0, extra = 4.6)`

**2a.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Write a function for your penalized NLL
from 1a and fit it with `optim(..., method = "BFGS")` at $\lambda = 0$
and $\lambda = 10$. Check: the temperature coefficient should be about
`r f2(b0[2])` at $\lambda = 0$ (the same as `glm()`) and `r f2(b10[2])`
at $\lambda = 10$. Fill in those two columns of the table.

```{r coef-table, fig.height=4.6}
rows <- lapply(c("water temp.", "elevation", "canopy", "conductivity", "area",
                 "fish", "bullfrogs", "road distance"),
               function(v) c(v, "", "", ""))
for (j in 1:8) rows[[j]][2:4] <- c(f2(b0[j + 1]), f2(b10[j + 1]), f2(b_lasso[j + 1]))
ans_cells <- lapply(1:8, function(j) c(FALSE, j > 1, j > 1, TRUE))
blank_table(c("Predictor", "MLE (lambda = 0)", "Ridge (lambda = 10)", "Lasso (2c)"),
            rows, col_widths = c(1.6, 1.3, 1.4, 1.2), row_height = 0.5, cex = 0.9,
            ans = ans_cells)
```

\ansbegin

```{r ridge-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, highlight=FALSE}
ridge_nll <- function(par, lambda) {
  p <- plogis(par[1] + X %*% par[-1])
  -sum(dbinom(ponds$bd_positive, ponds$frogs_swabbed, p, log = TRUE)) +
    lambda * sum(par[-1]^2)
}
optim(rep(0, 9), ridge_nll, lambda = 10, method = "BFGS")$par
```

\ansend

## Part 3: Interpret (~15 min)

**3a.** In your ridge path, what happens to the temperature and
elevation coefficients as $\lambda$ grows, compared with the other
predictors? Why?

\ansbegin

They move toward each other: temperature shrinks from `r f2(b0[2])`
while elevation grows from `r f2(b0[3])` to about `r f2(max(path[3, ]))`
before both shrink. The others shrink steadily toward 0. Temperature
and elevation are strongly correlated, and the ridge penalty
($\sum \beta_j^2$) is smaller when a shared effect is split between two
coefficients than when one carries it.

\ansend

`r nq(4, 5)`

**3b.** AIC's best model in Act 1 left out elevation, but the lasso
kept it. Use your Act 1 sketch to explain why the lasso kept both.

\ansbegin

As in the Act 1 sketch, the NLL contours for the two correlated
coefficients are long ellipses running parallel to an edge of the
lasso's diamond, so the lowest contour touches the edge partway along
it rather than at a corner. Both coefficients stay nonzero.

\ansend

`r nq(8, 6)`

## Reflection (~10 min)

The managers asked which pond features predict where Bd is common.
Write two or three sentences they could act on, including what these
data can and can't tell them about temperature versus elevation.

Also record any changes you made, new insights, and any "muddiest
points" or topics you want to review.

\ansbegin

Sample: Bd is more common in colder ponds, in ponds with bullfrogs, and
in more shaded ponds, so those are the ones to prioritize for
monitoring. These data can't say whether cold water itself or
something else about high elevation is responsible, because the two go
together; for choosing ponds, either one works.

\ansend

`r nq(5, 3)`
